ann_24.text: This part of the model acts on 206 of the 345 training cases, and 78 of those 206 are actually 'yes'.

For the typical case it acts on (a1 = 2, a2 = 3, a3 = 2, a4 = 2, a5 = 4, a6 = 2), it raises the predicted probability of 'yes' from about 72% without the part to above 99% with it (on the training data only).
Through this part, changing a6 from 1 to 2 clearly raises the predicted probability of 'yes' for the typical case from below 1% to above 99%.
Changing a3 from 1 to 2, or a1 from 1 to 2, also raises it from below 1% to above 99% (on the training data only).

Changing a1 from 1 to 3 clearly raises the predicted probability of 'yes' from below 1% to above 99% for the typical case with a3 = 1 or a6 = 1, while with a3 = 2 or a6 = 2 it is above 99% either way; this part is where that difference arises.
Through this part, giving a2 or a4 its first value slightly lowers the predicted probability of 'yes'.

ann_25.text: This part of the model acts on 259 of the 345 training cases, and 82 of those 259 are actually 'yes'.
For the typical case it acts on (a1 = 1, a2 = 1, a3 = 1, a4 = 2, a5 = 1, a6 = 1), it slightly changes the predicted probability of 'yes', which stays below 1% (on the training data only).
Through this part, a5 = 4 and a3 = 2 each slightly lower the predicted probability of 'yes' (on the training data only).

ann_26.text: This part of the model reads only a6 and barely changes the predictions.
It acts on the 168 training cases with a6 = 2, and 58 of them are actually 'yes'.
Through it, changing a6 from 1 to 2 slightly raises the predicted probability of 'yes' (on the training data only).

ann_27.text: Through this part, changing a1 from 1 to 3 clearly raises the predicted probability of 'yes' for the typical case from below 1% to above 99%, and changing a1 from 1 to 2 clearly raises it to about 75%.
Changing a5 from 1 to 2 raises it to about 93%, and from 1 to 3 to about 55% (on the training data only).
Changing a5 from 1 to 4 slightly raises it, to about 3% (on the training data only).
Giving a4 its first value, or changing a3 or a6 from 1 to 2, slightly lowers it, and changing a2 from 3 to 1 or to 2 slightly raises it (on the training data only).

ann_28.text: For the typical case, changing a1 from 1 to 2 clearly raises the predicted probability of 'yes' from below 1% to above 99%.
Changing a5 from 1 to 2 raises it to about 93%, and from 1 to 3 to about 55% (on the training data only).
Changing a5 from 1 to 4 raises it only slightly, to about 1% (on the training data only).
Giving a4 its first value slightly lowers it, and changing a2 from 3 to 2 slightly raises it; both leave the typical case below 1%.

ann_24.original: Hypothesis: a falling count ramp over first-value indicators. In indicator terms node 263 = ReLU(18.98 - 8.46[a2=1] - 9.29[a3=1] - 6.75[a4=1] - 8.23[a6=1] + 5.81[a1=2] - 24.11[a1=3]); a3:2 and a6:2 enter as complements of a3=1, a6=1. a1=1: positive iff at most two of {a2,a3,a4,a6}=1 (all pairs >= 1.23, all triples <= -4.46). a1=2: +5.8 shift, three indicators leave it at 0.3-1.4 except a2+a3+a6 (-1.19); four switch it off. a1=3: always 0 (max pre -5.13). a5 is not consulted. Evidence (train, n=345): closed form from get_formula (z-scored inputs; closed-form max err 0.041 from 3-s.f. rounding); sensitivity largest for a1:3 (6.66); values 0..24.79, zero on 40.3% of rows; ablation flips 112/345 decisions and drops logit AUC 0.734 -> 0.537. Readout 5.14: the dominant decision-bearing term.
ann_24.proposed: This part acts on 206 training cases and raises their predicted probability of 'yes'; through it, moving a6, a3 or a1 away from its first value takes the typical case from below 1% to above 99%, and the effect of a1 = 3 depends on a3 and a6.

ann_25.original: Hypothesis: an a5-not-4 indicator weighted by a3. Node 1855 = ReLU(0.295 + 0.682[a3=1] - 3.271[a5=4]) takes values 0 (a5=4), 0.295 (a3=2) or 0.977 (a3=1). Evidence (train, n=345): closed form (err 0.0026 from rounding); sensitivity a5:4 1.06 vs a3:1 0.26; readout 1.53 adds at most 1.49 to the logit; ablation flips 3/345 decisions, logit AUC 0.7335 -> 0.7329. A minor correction term.
ann_25.proposed: A small correction: through this part, a5 = 4 and a3 = 2 slightly lower the predicted probability of 'yes' (on the training data only).

ann_26.original: Hypothesis: a near-inert a6 indicator. Node 3471 = ReLU(0.743 - 1.412[a6=1]) = 0.743[a6=2], linear in binary a6. Evidence (train, n=345): closed form (err 0.0003); readout 0.105 adds at most 0.078 to the logit; ablation flips no decisions. Functionally negligible, unearned structure.
ann_26.proposed: This part reads only a6 and barely changes the predictions.

ann_27.original: Hypothesis: the direct linear part. Per attribute in indicator terms (relative to the reference value): a1=1 -15.69, a1=3 +24.94 (a1=2: 0); a5=1 -14.80, a5=2 +2.38, a5=4 -3.58 (a5=3: 0); a4=1 -4.90; a3=2 -2.19; a2=1 +1.20, a2=2 +0.73, a2=3 +0.61; a6=2 -0.24. It penalises the two first values the ramp does not see (a1=1, a5=1) by ~15 each, and gives a1=3 a +24.9 bonus that keeps every a1=3 input positive although the ramp is off there. Evidence (train, n=345): closed form (linear; err 0.065 from 3-s.f. rounding on values -33.4..+32.2); sensitivities equal the z-scale weights (a1:3 11.5, a1:1 7.5, a5:1 6.4).
ann_27.proposed: This part raises the predicted probability of 'yes' when a1 moves from 1 to 3 (to above 99%) or to 2 (to about 75%), and, on the training data only, when a5 moves from 1 to 2 or 3, with small effects of the other attributes.

ann_28.original: Hypothesis: additive composition under the output sigmoid, logit = 2.58 + Linear + 5.14*Ramp + 1.53*A5not4 + 0.105*A6. a4:2, a4:3, a5:3 have no enabled connections (zero-effect entries). The model is an upper-edge-only count detector: for a1 in {1,2} it is positive while few attributes take their first value and negative once about three of {a2,a3,a4,a6} (a1=1) or four (a1=2) do; a5=1 counts only through Linear's -14.8, which is not enough to flip a1=1 inputs with one other first value. There is no lower edge: inputs with zero or one first value get the largest logits. a1=3 inputs are all positive (107/107 on train) via Linear's +24.9. Evidence (train, n=345): positive rate by (a1, count) - a1=1: count<=2 100%, 3 74%, >=4 0%; a1=2: count<=3 100%, 4 29%, 5 0%; a1=3: 100% at every count. Predicts positive on 85.5% of train rows (accuracy 0.472 at 0.5). Logits reach |~130| so the sigmoid saturates; the sigmoid-output AUC 0.807 is inflated by ties at 1.0, the logit ranking AUC is 0.734. Compared with the MONK-2 target (exactly two first values): the network captures only the upper edge (>=3-4 first values -> negative) and none of the lower edge (0-1 -> negative), and ignores the count entirely when a1=3.
ann_28.proposed: For the typical case the model turns to 'yes' when a1 changes from 1 to 2, and, on the training data only, when a5 changes from 1 to 2 or 3 but hardly when it changes to 4.

summary.text: For the typical case (the most common value of each attribute: a1 = 1, a2 = 3, a3 = 1, a4 = 2, a5 = 1, a6 = 1), changing a1 from 1 to 2 clearly raises the predicted probability of 'yes' from below 1% to above 99%.
Changing a5 from 1 to 2 raises it to about 93%, and from 1 to 3 to about 55% (on the training data only).
Changing a5 from 1 to 4 raises it only slightly, to about 1% (on the training data only).

Changing a1 from 1 to 3 clearly raises the predicted probability of 'yes' from below 1% to above 99% for the typical case with a3 = 1 or a6 = 1, while with a3 = 2 or a6 = 2 it is above 99% either way.
Giving a4 its first value slightly lowers the predicted probability of 'yes', and changing a2 from 3 to 2 slightly raises it, with the typical case staying below 1%.
One small part of the model, which reads only a6, barely changes the predictions.

worth_checking.flag: model does not follow the exactly-two rule
worth_checking.text: Worth checking: the typical case has four attributes at their first value (a1, a3, a5 and a6), and moving just one of them away (a1 from 1 to 2, or a6 from 1 to 2 through one part) clearly raises the predicted probability of 'yes' from below 1% to above 99%, although the case then has three attributes at their first value, which the exactly-two rule counts as 'no'.

worth_checking.flag: attribute values other than the first matter
worth_checking.text: Worth checking: the model separates the values of a5 other than the first: for the typical case, a5 = 2 gives a predicted probability of 'yes' of about 93%, a5 = 3 about 55% and a5 = 4 about 1% (on the training data only); through one part, a1 = 2 gives about 75% and a1 = 3 above 99%.

parts.name: upper_edge_count_classifier
parts.original_hypothesis: Hypothesis: additive composition under the output sigmoid, logit = 2.58 + Linear + 5.14*Ramp + 1.53*A5not4 + 0.105*A6. a4:2, a4:3, a5:3 have no enabled connections (zero-effect entries). The model is an upper-edge-only count detector: for a1 in {1,2} it is positive while few attributes take their first value and negative once about three of {a2,a3,a4,a6} (a1=1) or four (a1=2) do; a5=1 counts only through Linear's -14.8, which is not enough to flip a1=1 inputs with one other first value. There is no lower edge: inputs with zero or one first value get the largest logits. a1=3 inputs are all positive (107/107 on train) via Linear's +24.9. Evidence (train, n=345): positive rate by (a1, count) - a1=1: count<=2 100%, 3 74%, >=4 0%; a1=2: count<=3 100%, 4 29%, 5 0%; a1=3: 100% at every count. Predicts positive on 85.5% of train rows (accuracy 0.472 at 0.5). Logits reach |~130| so the sigmoid saturates; the sigmoid-output AUC 0.807 is inflated by ties at 1.0, the logit ranking AUC is 0.734. Compared with the MONK-2 target (exactly two first values): the network captures only the upper edge (>=3-4 first values -> negative) and none of the lower edge (0-1 -> negative), and ignores the count entirely when a1=3.

parts.name: few_first_values_ramp
parts.original_hypothesis: Hypothesis: a falling count ramp over first-value indicators. In indicator terms node 263 = ReLU(18.98 - 8.46[a2=1] - 9.29[a3=1] - 6.75[a4=1] - 8.23[a6=1] + 5.81[a1=2] - 24.11[a1=3]); a3:2 and a6:2 enter as complements of a3=1, a6=1. a1=1: positive iff at most two of {a2,a3,a4,a6}=1 (all pairs >= 1.23, all triples <= -4.46). a1=2: +5.8 shift, three indicators leave it at 0.3-1.4 except a2+a3+a6 (-1.19); four switch it off. a1=3: always 0 (max pre -5.13). a5 is not consulted. Evidence (train, n=345): closed form from get_formula (z-scored inputs; closed-form max err 0.041 from 3-s.f. rounding); sensitivity largest for a1:3 (6.66); values 0..24.79, zero on 40.3% of rows; ablation flips 112/345 decisions and drops logit AUC 0.734 -> 0.537. Readout 5.14: the dominant decision-bearing term.

parts.name: direct_linear
parts.original_hypothesis: Hypothesis: the direct linear part. Per attribute in indicator terms (relative to the reference value): a1=1 -15.69, a1=3 +24.94 (a1=2: 0); a5=1 -14.80, a5=2 +2.38, a5=4 -3.58 (a5=3: 0); a4=1 -4.90; a3=2 -2.19; a2=1 +1.20, a2=2 +0.73, a2=3 +0.61; a6=2 -0.24. It penalises the two first values the ramp does not see (a1=1, a5=1) by ~15 each, and gives a1=3 a +24.9 bonus that keeps every a1=3 input positive although the ramp is off there. Evidence (train, n=345): closed form (linear; err 0.065 from 3-s.f. rounding on values -33.4..+32.2); sensitivities equal the z-scale weights (a1:3 11.5, a1:1 7.5, a5:1 6.4).

parts.name: a5_not4_unit
parts.original_hypothesis: Hypothesis: an a5-not-4 indicator weighted by a3. Node 1855 = ReLU(0.295 + 0.682[a3=1] - 3.271[a5=4]) takes values 0 (a5=4), 0.295 (a3=2) or 0.977 (a3=1). Evidence (train, n=345): closed form (err 0.0026 from rounding); sensitivity a5:4 1.06 vs a3:1 0.26; readout 1.53 adds at most 1.49 to the logit; ablation flips 3/345 decisions, logit AUC 0.7335 -> 0.7329. A minor correction term.

parts.name: a6_tiny_unit
parts.original_hypothesis: Hypothesis: a near-inert a6 indicator. Node 3471 = ReLU(0.743 - 1.412[a6=1]) = 0.743[a6=2], linear in binary a6. Evidence (train, n=345): closed form (err 0.0003); readout 0.105 adds at most 0.078 to the logit; ablation flips no decisions. Functionally negligible, unearned structure.

reference_patient.definition: the typical patient: the median training patient for every number and the most common training category for every category (not a real patient)

confidence_rules.clearly: a meaningful change in predicted risk for a typical patient (at least 5% points), the test split agrees (same sign, and its bootstrap interval over test patients excludes no benefit), and every group has at least 20 training patients
confidence_rules.consistently across patients: the claim holds for at least 90% of training patients (range across patients); this is not a significance statement
confidence_rules.on the training data only: the test split disagrees (opposite sign, or no benefit on test patients) or is unclear (its interval includes no benefit), or no test check is available
confidence_rules.slightly: the change in predicted risk for a typical patient is below 5% points
confidence_rules.the model has little data on this: a compared group has fewer than 20 training patients

settings.effect_scale: log-odds (output pre-activation) for verification; predicted risk for the typical patient for wording

summary.text: For a typical case, the model gives a clearly higher predicted probability of 'yes' if a1 = 2 (above 99%) than if a1 = 1 (below 1%).
For a typical case, the model gives a higher predicted probability of 'yes' if a5 = 2 (about 93%) than if a5 = 1 (below 1%) (on the training data only).
For a typical case, the model gives a higher predicted probability of 'yes' if a5 = 3 (about 55%) than if a5 = 1 (below 1%) (on the training data only).

The model gives a clearly higher predicted probability of 'yes' if a1 = 3 than if a1 = 1, and even more so if a3 = 1: for a typical case, going from a1 = 1 to a1 = 3 moves the predicted probability of 'yes' from below 1% to above 99% if a3 = 1, and from above 99% to above 99% if a3 = 2.

This changes the prediction only slightly: for a typical case, going from a3 = 1 to a3 = 2 moves the predicted probability of 'yes' from about 1% to above 99% if a5 = 4, and from below 1% to above 99% if attribute a5 is something other than a5 = 4 (on the training data only).
